schools.summary: Ellicott holds the text of the second verse exceedingly corrupt, prefers the ancient versions' first person, and denies that the thought of merit could have been the original sense, since the good in question means happiness and not conduct; Keil and Delitzsch find a writer in danger of death whose cry for help is swallowed up by a settled calm and a bright hope.

Clarke is convinced that every verse of the psalm belongs to Jesus Christ and none other, reads the opening as the prayer of the man Christ Jesus in the garden, and notes that the name used is the one signifying the strong God; Wesley takes the second verse to mean that God is not capable of any advantage from our service.

Calvin reports the Jewish expositors divided over the title, between a psalm fit to be written in letters of gold and one fit to be engraven on a durable pillar; Gill takes the prayer as proper to Christ as man and defends the supplied words of the address from the Targum and the Jewish commentators.

Henry takes the golden sense of the title because the psalm speaks so plainly of Christ and his resurrection, and reads David first with Christ by application; Spurgeon presses the second verse to its limit, that God would have been inconceivably glorious had the race perished and no atonement been offered.
Augustine reads the whole as the words of our King, speaking in the character of the human nature he assumed.

debates.issue: Whose voice speaks in the psalm

positions.view: Clarke holds that every verse belongs to Jesus Christ and none other, some parts never having applied to David.
Augustine has our King speak throughout in the character of the human nature he assumed.
Henry reads David first and Christ by application, noting at each turn where the verse is applicable to him.
Keil and Delitzsch keep to David throughout, a friend of God in danger of death whose confidence is unshaken.

debates.issue: Whether the clause about goodness not extending to God can bear the sense given it

positions.view: Henry and Spurgeon build on it the doctrine that God has no need of our services and is happy without us, so that we can merit nothing.
Ellicott holds the text corrupt, the words about the soul a mere gloss, and the thought of merit impossible in the original, since the good meant is happiness and not conduct.

outliers.view: That the title's meaning is genuinely undecided among the Jewish expositors, between letters of gold and an inscription on a pillar, and need not be settled to read the psalm.

themes: David or Christ as the speaker
my goodness extendeth not to thee
1.pericope_label: Preserve me, O God: thou art my Lord, my goodness extendeth not to thee

schools.summary: Gill makes the saints those set apart by the Father, expiated by the blood of Christ and sanctified by the Spirit, and explains the phrase about the earth as marking the place of their abode rather than distinguishing them from the saints in heaven.

Henry makes it a standing requirement that saints on earth we must be or we shall never be saints in heaven, and holds the paradox that the excellent ones are sometimes so poor that they need our goodness extended to them; he also supplies the epigram that whoever thinks one God too little will find two too many and yet hundreds not enough.

Clarke suggests the apostles, or even the angels, and applies the multiplied sorrows to those still seeking another Messiah; Wesley refuses the Christological reference at this verse, since the goodness of Christ was principally designed for sinners.

Ellicott calls the verse unintelligible as it stands, proposes an emendation making the saints themselves the excellent, renders the next verse of those who change to another god, and finds in the libations of blood the rites of Moloch and Chemosh.
Augustine reads the earth of the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem, whose conversation is fixed by the anchor of hope in that country although they are as yet conversant in the flesh here.

debates.issue: Whether this verse speaks of Christ or of David

positions.view: Wesley grants the sense but refuses the reference, since it agrees more properly with David than with Christ, whose goodness was imparted to sinners.
Clarke keeps the Messianic reading and makes the saints the first planters of Christianity, with the angels perhaps included.

themes: the saints that are in the earth
3.pericope_label: The saints that are in the earth: their sorrows shall be multiplied that hasten after another god

schools.summary: Gill reads the portion against the Levitical priests who had no inheritance in Canaan but had the Lord for their part, and argues that the pleasant places are persons rather than places, the chosen ones given to Christ as his portion.

Henry draws the rule that gracious persons, though they still covet more of God, never covet more than God, and that those whose lot is cast in a land of light may say the lines have fallen pleasantly, much more those who have Immanuel's love and not only Immanuel's land; Spurgeon finds that obedience itself led into pleasant places, the joy set before Christ sending its splendour down the rugged way of the cross.

Clarke makes the lot given the Messiah the redemption of mankind, the cup a cup of suffering drunk for their sake through which he imparts the cup of consolation, and the heritage an inheritance of immortal spirits; Wesley keeps the plainer image of a feast where each guest had his portion allotted him.

Ellicott imagines the poet exiled from his inheritance and consoled by a better part that cannot be taken from him, and explains that God does not merely cast a man's lot but holds it fast; Keil and Delitzsch make the charming district into which the lines fall the fellowship of God itself.

debates.issue: Whether the pleasant places are places or persons

positions.view: Gill argues for persons, the lines marking out the chosen ones given to Christ, and notes that the word for places is a supplement made by two Jewish commentators.
Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch keep the land, the measuring cords falling because the measured portions were distributed by lot.

themes: the Lord as portion and cup
the lines fallen in pleasant places
5.pericope_label: The Lord is the portion of mine inheritance: I have a goodly heritage

schools.summary: Gill assigns thanksgiving to Christ as man and Mediator, and guards the object of the setting, which is not the fear of God only nor the book of the law but the Lord himself.

Henry makes conscience the instructor of the night season, admonishing a man about the duties arising from his choice, and records that the apostle's use of these verses lets them be applied to all Christians; Spurgeon adds that the fear of death once cast its shadow over the Redeemer, who was strengthened by an angel and stayed not his hand until it was finished.

Clarke dwells on the kidneys, hidden in fat and burnt in sacrifice to signify that the soul's most secret purposes are to be devoted to God, and takes the night seasons for the time of the passion; Wesley marks this verse as the point where David is carried above himself to speak as a type of Christ.

Ellicott prefers to render the verb as warning rather than instructing, conscience echoing the voice of God with a root that carries obligation; Keil and Delitzsch find in heart, glory and flesh the spirit, soul and body of the apostle's prayer, expressed here as confident expectation.

positions.view: Wesley locates the turn here, since hitherto David seems to have spoken of himself but is now transported by the spirit of prophecy.
Clarke recognises no turn, having held from the first that the whole psalm belongs to Christ alone.

themes: the reins instructing in the night season
I have set the Lord always before me
the apostle's use of these verses
7.pericope_label: I will bless the Lord, who hath given me counsel: I have set the Lord always before me

schools.summary: Gill rules out the place of the damned, where Christ never went, concludes that the word is best read of the grave, and takes the path of life for the resurrection shown to Christ by his being raised, the firstfruits of them that slept.

Clarke states that there is no sense in which these words can be spoken of David, holds that the rest in the grave was long enough to prove the death real but too short for corruption, argues from the versions and the manuscripts that the plural of the holy ones is a corruption, and reads the pleasures as an eternal progression; Wesley sets our momentary pleasures against the pleasures of immortal souls enjoying an eternal God.

Ellicott renders the word usually given as corruption by a pit, making the clauses synonyms for dying, warns against seeing a conscious reference to immortality here, and yet finds the first faint scintillation of that light, which justifies the use made of the passage in the New Testament.

debates.issue: Whether the closing verses can be spoken of David at all

positions.view: Clarke denies it flatly, and rests the resurrection argument on the word for corruption.
Ellicott renders that word a pit, so that the verse only says God will not abandon his beloved to death, while granting that a larger hope is stirring in it.

debates.issue: Whether the holy one of the tenth verse is singular or plural

positions.view: Clarke finds the singular in several ancient editions and many collated manuscripts and twice in the apostle's quotation, and takes the plural for a corruption or an emphatic singular.
Ellicott adds that the received text's own margin calls the sign of the plural superfluous, and finds the weight of authority for the singular.

outliers.view: That the psalmist had no conscious doctrine of immortality here, and that the New Testament use of the passage is nevertheless justified by the larger hope stirring in it.

themes: my flesh shall rest in hope
thou wilt not leave my soul in hell
9.pericope_label: My flesh shall rest in hope: thou wilt shew me the path of life
